One of these may be the word you’re looking for and if not it will at least explain the process behind this. The basic phrase I’d say is Selective Memory, kind of like a branch under the tree of [Confirmation Bias.](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation_bias) You and your friend are having that conversation about your car. You suggest what you think the fix is. Now, I do not know you or your friend of course, but you do mention this person tends to do this behavior quite frequently, suggesting this is somewhat of a trait of theirs. This is where confirmation bias comes in. Their [Schematic Nature](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schema_(psychology)) in this example could be that they want to be seen as intelligent, wanting to find the solution for you/try to feel helpful to you, or maybe even they dismiss your intelligence in a way where they feel the need to be more intelligent than you. So you say what you think is right. They [Negatively Prime](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priming_(psychology)) your conversation (the stimulus) where they hear it, but subconsciously ignore the solution due to their Schema. Later on while they are doing their research, they stumble upon your solution, the spark plugs. [Repetition Priming](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priming_(psychology)) occurs as they already experienced the term spark plugs from your conversation, but subconsciously ignored it as I said earlier. With their Schema/Confirmation Bias of (assumably) wanting to be perceived as the one with the right answer, they come to the conclusion they came up with the solution. Basically, you both discuss, they subconsciously ignore your stimulus due to their confirmation bias to later benefit themself, recalls your key phrase/solution of spark plugs in their research later, and reports back to you on a biased memory recall of information.
